To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the work content of correlations is not a monotonically decreasing function of the distance between the system and the ancilla and that, in general, the work that can extracted from correlations is not the same as the work that can extract the correlation itself.

(i) work can be extracted from both classical and non-classical correlations between a quantum system and an ancilla, (ii) the work content of the correlations is not necessarily equal to their mutual information, and (iii) the work content is not necessarily equal for different quantum states of the same system, even if they have the same mutual information.

the work that can potentially be extracted from a system in a nonequilibrium state depends on how the system is measured, and that the optimal measurement protocol for extracting work from correlations is not necessarily the one that maximally disturbs the state of the system.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental question of whether and how work can be extracted from quantum correlations.
the role of quantum correlations in thermodynamics, with particular emphasis on the interplay between work extraction and quantum measurements.
the thermodynamic implications of quantum measurements and quantum correlations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the work content of quantum correlations cannot be extracted without a nonlocal measurement.
quantum discord can only be extracted by performing a non-local measurement, which is in agreement with the fact that it cannot be accessed by local operations.
the thermodynamic cost of quantum measurements depends on the type of quantum correlations that are being measured, with the most costly measurements being those that extract quantum correlations.

the optimal tradeoff between the work content and the work extraction efficiency is given by the quantum discord, and this tradeoff is the same as that between the quantum mutual information and the quantum mutual information gain.

the thermodynamic cost of quantum measurements and correlations is not only a function of the initial and final quantum states, but also of the specific measurement protocol used to access the work.
